name: Sprocket
text: We should implement the A/B test on a voluntary cohort where users opt into the feed changes. This approach respects user autonomy, likely leading to more genuine engagement and reliable feedback, which aligns with our quality-first principle. The trade-off is that we may receive a smaller sample size, narrowing the breadth of data, but the insights gained from willing participants will be more meaningful. This decision allows us to focus on quality interactions over sheer volume.

name: Gauge
text: The real risk isn’t limited data—it’s that a voluntary cohort *self-selects*, skewing results toward users who already prefer the changes. A forced A/B split with random assignment avoids this bias but risks churn if the new feed underperforms. Settle it by running a small, randomized pilot first—measure churn *and* engagement—before scaling.

name: Sprocket
text:
Run a small, randomized pilot with 5% of users forced into the new feed for one week. This gives us clean, unbiased data on actual impact without risking mass churn. The trade-off is that 5% of users will have a worse experience if the feed underperforms—but that’s a controlled risk we can mitigate with a quick rollback.

name: Gauge
text: Gauge: A 5% forced pilot still risks churn if the new feed underperforms, and the "controlled risk" isn’t zero—users who hate the change may never return, skewing long-term metrics. Instead, run a 5% *opt-in* pilot first to measure baseline engagement, then force the remaining 5% only if the opt-in group shows no churn. Settle it by comparing retention rates between opt-in and forced cohorts after two weeks.

name: Ratchet
text: DECISION: Run a 5% opt-in pilot for one week to measure baseline engagement, then proceed with a forced 5% split test if metrics show positive engagement; ownership lies with the product lead.
